incidents.cause: The loss of main rotor power due to a main rotor transmission failure from a lack of lubrication.

A partial loss of engine power during cruise flight due to loose “B” nut fittings and a bent tube as a result of maintenance personnel’s inadequate inspection of the nuts during the most recent inspection.
A loose fuel line fitting that resulted in a partial loss of engine power during the initial takeoff climb.  Contributing to the accident was inadequate maintenance installation of the fitting.
A flight control malfunction due to either a hydraulic hardover or a flight control stiffness event, which resulted in a loss of control.
A total loss of engine power due to the failure of the No. 2 bearing, which resulted from a fractured separator.
The pilot's failure to maintain control while landing in a high density altitude environment due to a loss of tail rotor effectiveness.
The pilot’s failure to maintain an appropriate descent rate for a glassy water landing, which resulted in a hard landing.
The pilot’s failure to maintain a stabilized approach, which resulted in a bounced landing and subsequent go-around with insufficient distance to clear trees during the climb.
A loss of engine power due to fuel contamination.
The pilot's inadequate compensation for wind conditions during the aborted takeoff.
The pilot's failure to maintain airplane control during a go-around in gusting tailwind conditions, which resulted in a collision with trees.
an inadvertent encounter with convective turbulence that resulted in a flight attendant injury.
The airplane’s encounter with severe turbulence.

The captain’s pitch up input to avoid an overspeed condition, which resulted in a flight attendant falling and fracturing her ankle. Contributing was the airplane’s excessive airspeed during the transition to the automation-managed descent profile.

A high pressure turbine 2nd stage blade separation due to stress corrosion cracking in the J channel cooling cavity.
